utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Kehoe objects to my writing, he certainly would have objected to my predrafting the document, but with all respect to my learned friend across the bar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And all the respect I owe to Mr. Kehoe as well, I have to overrule the objection. We have to have a clear vision of what we are doing as to answers and questions. I simply wanted to say that in the future, I would have preferred a more effective method to use, but now we will have Mr. Hayman going to be writing, asking questions, writing it down, it is going to take some time. If we could have done it differently it would have been better, but it is too bad. Since we are talking about Mr. Hayman writing, I do not see any problem with that. Mr. Hayman will write it, then it will be tendered as evidence, but we have to also note specifically and very clearly are the witness's answers and any other questions that Mr. Kehoe will want to ask. Mr. Hayman if you have no other documents you wish to produce, perhaps you should do this quickly, that is to describe the command levels so that we can get to the crux of the matter, which is the answers from Colonel Watters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like to, your Honour. Colonel Watters, first of all, would you agree that the level of command at which Colonel Blaskic was located in 1993 was that of the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Central Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Which we could represent by "operative zone"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Below the operative zone level, would you agree that the next level of command in the command structure of the HVO in place at the time was that of the operative group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I explained this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that under the operative group comes the brigade, or a number of brigades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Under the brigades, are there battalions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never really understood it as that, because the size of the brigade could be -- by and large villages were named as brigades or brigades named after people. The size of the brigades depended very much on the size of the village or area that the brigade was raised from. We never focused below brigade, which we considered to be the tactical level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: During your tour in the theatre, did you hear the use of the term "Boyna" to refer to a unit of soldiers, B-O-Y-N-A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no memory of it. I might have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the military structure of your military, would you agree that the battalion comes under the brigade in terms of the structure or command structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then, your Honour, I am going to put battalion down as a general representation of military structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you have an objection you wish to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with Mr. Kehoe. This is not what the witness said. Mr. Hayman, this is the disadvantage of the method you are using. It would have been better for you to prepare the document, give it to the witness, which would have gone more quickly. Now for each of the points you are going to ask questions and you have to wait until you get the answer that you are looking for. If this document is to be put in as an exhibit, it must be clearly marked, putting in question marks where it would be that the witness does not agree with your definition of brigade as you explained it. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is fine, your Honour, but this illustrates why I could not prepare the exhibit in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Not at all, I do not agree with that. You could have put in a document and the witness would have made comments, it would have gone much more quickly. It does not work for brigade. There is something which is not accepted there and I sustain the objection of the Prosecutor and whatever questions that the witness has, it has to be indicated on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let us go back, Colonel. Operative zone, that is a level of command you know to have existed in the HVO in, for example, 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then I am going to place next to "operative zone", "(HVO)"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And the same with respect to the operative group formation, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You know brigades, at least the term brigade, to have been used by the HVO, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How would you describe the command structure, that is the existence of units with commanders within the HVO during the period of your tour of duty below the brigade level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not actually aware of a structure that was below brigade level. I did not deal below brigade level, and when studying the daily reports, as one village appeared to be attacking another village, we did not, at the battalion operational level, involve ourselves in the structure of the village force, the brigade. That is not to say that through reports we might not have put together structures that we would have processed through Mil Info Summs, but I would not actually have involved myself in the detail of that, at battalion level. Our company commanders might have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us whether there were smaller units of organisation such as based on a territorial principle within the HVO in 1993 under the brigade level, or do you simply not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Sorry, the one exception to that would be the unit that you talked about earlier, in the bungalows, which appeared to be a small, self-contained unit and I never penetrated exactly which of the brigades it belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So there were other smaller units, but you cannot further describe them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the only one that I ever identified personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you, if a military action was to be ordered at the level of operative zone, for example an action to attack military targets and eliminate military targets in Kruscica, Stari Vitez, Ahmici and other locations where there were military targets, what would that order look like? What kinds of elements would be contained in that order at the level of the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw an order promulgated at the operatal zone. I can only tell you how I would imagine it would be, because most of the senior officers within the HVO had been former JNA officer, and had been trained formerly in military doctrine. I would imagine that it would give specific mission statement and specific tasks to subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: For example: "Subordinate unit X, you are to attack BiH military positions in Kruscica and eliminate them"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, that is what I would write.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Based on your 25 years of military experience, that is the type of order you would expect coming from the operative zone level, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about at the level of the operative group? Would it be any more detailed at the operative group level, or not? That is the order, for example, to attack military targets and eliminate or neutralise them in the village of Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, essentially what you are talking about is the allocation of resources to tasks, so at the operational zone a specific area controlled by the operational group would be given a series of tasks. It would be up to the operational group commander to allocate his resources to achieve the task set by him, by the operational zone. That process cascades down through brigade, and the brigade would organise its forces in whatever groupings it had and give people specific tasks, down to which side of the road, left or right, particular groups would assault a position, where the fire bases would be, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Just slow down for just a moment. The operative group order, is it correct, would likely allocate resources at the brigade level among the different tasks which comprised the overall mission or goal set forth at the operative zone level, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then at the brigade level, for example, with that order, under the situation we are discussing, the scenario or hypothetical if you will, the brigade order would specifically target resources or allocate resources to, for example, three different --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Manoeuvre units, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Manoeuvre units to attack one village at three different locations or perhaps two villages, something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Based on your general military experience, is that the end of the chain of orders, or are there further more detailed orders to lower level and smaller units of soldiers, telling them what their task is and what they are to do in fulfilling the overall order from above?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only explain from the British army's doctrine and that would be the case. The battalion commander would give orders to his company commanders. The company commander gives orders to the platoon commanders, a platoon is three ten-man manoeuvre units, and the section commander, the ten-man manoeuvre unit, would give orders to his two fire teams, each of four men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So at least within the military structure from your tradition, there are four additional levels of command below the brigade level, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, to achieve the mission statement at each level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is battalion level, company level, platoon level and section level, roughly units of ten men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge and training and experience, would you agree that at the battalion level, which you described as being one below the brigade level, that typically a battalion order would typically, for example, direct an attack or an assault on one location, one hill, one village, something of that sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it would really depend on the strength of the enemy, and in attack you would want to establish probably a three-to-one ratio, so, dependent on the strength of the enemy position, would probably depend the size of force you committed to it. A battalion, if it was attacking three platoon locations, might allocate a company to attack each platoon. If a battalion was attacking a company defence position on a hill, then the battalion would attack it as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Coming down below the battalion level and the company level to the platoon level, would it be common, for example, in fighting in built-up areas, for a platoon commander to give an order to his units, his 30 or so men, to secure a group of buildings or a single building within a built-up area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the company plan, within the battalion plan, within the brigade plan, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How about at the lowest level --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, could you try to summarise where you are getting? I would like us to go a little more quickly. We are going through a military course here, very interesting, of course, to show that there was a command chain from the commander down to the platoons to the soldiers. What are you getting at? Let us try to get there as directly as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I will -- I will move as quickly as I can. What we are trying to establish is the nature of the orders that would be given at each level in this chain and at the operative zone level, as the witness has described, basically a mission is set forth, but the decisions of how that is to be carried out, what resources are to be allocated where, and as we will see in a moment whether a particular building is or is not to be attacked, those decisions are made, five, six, seven levels of command below the level of the operative zone. That is the line of enquiry I am pursuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The witness answered you, answered you quickly. He said it depended on the force of the enemy, if it was an important zone, if there was great potential for the enemy, if he had a great ability to resist. Obviously his resource allegation would be given to more important commands for various situations. It is part of military logic it seems to me. Go ahead, but try to go about it more quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the context of fighting in built-up areas, Colonel, at what level in these seven or so levels of command that you have set forth would a decision be made whether a particular structure represented a military target and whether a grenade should be thrown into that structure prior to entering? At what level of command would that decision be made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who was to attack which house would obviously depend on the size of the force attacking, which would be predicated by the size of the resistance you were expecting. When you get down to the actual assaulting of a specific house within the plan of the platoon commander, the company commander, the battalion commander, the actual house would probably be attacked by a section of ten men, and as to the throwing of a grenade into a house, that would be the decision of probably the section commander when he came up with his tactical plan as to how the section would assault the house. He would decide which soldiers would put down the initial fire, which soldiers would enter the house and the individual soldier would throw the grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Has counsel completed with his chart?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have completed my work with that tablet, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you wish to have it admitted into evidence, the first three lines, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It is not necessary, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Colonel Watters, on 19th April 1993, did you receive a report from one of your call signs of HVO artillery firing from the artillery location at Mosunj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, we had hundreds of reports of artillery fire over that period. I cannot be specific as to one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At approximately 12.30 pm on 19th April, do you have any recollection of receiving a report of the firing of an HVO artillery at Mosunj, that being approximately the time at which the city of Zenica received a number of shells, artillery shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I stated yesterday, we cross-referenced reports of firing at approximately the time we were told that the artillery shells landed in Zenica. There were examples where they cross matched. I cannot remember what they were. That in itself did not mean those guns actually fired at Zenica, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In your prior interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, did you indicate or tell them: "Our call signs reported HVO artillery firing from the Mosunj feature at 12.30, grid reference 1994", that being a reference to 19th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have had a lot of conversations with the Prosecution counsel. When cross-referencing Mil Info Summs and situation reports, I may have been able to establish that. I apologise that I cannot recall the detail right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So if you said that and you had those materials before you now, you believe you could answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I probably could. As I said, we did cross-reference and there were examples of HVO artillery firing at the reported time of the rounds falling in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was any overall report or summary of that incident or event prepared by UNPROFOR, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was recorded in a Mil Info Summ, the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said earlier that you visited the Serb artillery positions on the Vlasik feature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not say I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did someone else visit that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said Colonel Stewart spoke to the Serb regional commander that controlled that artillery on Vlasik mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you tell us that Colonel Stewart determined that the Serb artillery on the Vlasik feature could not reach Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a vague memory that it had 17 kilometres range when our people checked the type of artillery they had but 17 kilometres was not in range of Zenica. Again, I am recalling a conversation four years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You were aware during your tour of duty that the Serbs were regularly shelling Zenica during the time period of April and May 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not aware that the Serbs were regularly shelling Zenica. The fall of artillery on Zenica on the 18th was a cataclysmic event. They might have been shelling the areas around, but not the city itself. I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If they were, would that be inconsistent with the report that Colonel Stewart gave you, that the Serb artillery on the Vlasik feature was out of range of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, can you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If in fact the Serbs were shelling Zenica, and did shell Zenica on a number of occasions in April and May 1993, would that be inconsistent with the representation, the information that Colonel Stewart gave you, that he had determined that the Serb positions on the Vlasik feature could not reach Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only two recollections I have of artillery falling on Zenica were on the 18th and 24th April. I have no recollection of any other, that is the first point. Secondly, in theoretical terms, had artillery which could have been unequivocally traced to the Serbs been falling on Zenica, then we would have not been accurate in our assumption that the Vlasik mountain could not reach Zenica, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let us return for a moment to the group of soldiers that dressed in black and that were based in the Swiss chalet near Nadioci. Do you have them in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Based on your experience in the theatre, did you determine that they appeared to respond to a higher authority than Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what higher authority that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We thought they responded on a dual military and political chain of command, and we assessed that their political chain of command was possibly Mr. Dario Kordic in Busovaca, and that was reinforced by the capturing of the aid convoy, but that was the only incident we have to support that hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know an individual named Nick Iljic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was he a member of 1 Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not prepared to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- I take it you decline to answer the question of whether he was a soldier with the 1 Cheshires in Bosnia, is that right? I just want to make clear what you are and are not willing to say to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are straying potentially into an area about which by the law of the United Kingdom the Colonel is not permitted to discuss. If the court wants to go into private session, I will gladly elaborate on what the Colonel is permitted by United Kingdom law to say and not say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, why do I not finish the rest of my examination and then over the lunch hour perhaps I can discuss this with the Prosecutor? There may be a more efficient resolution to the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with Mr. Hayman. Complete your cross-examination and the question may possibly be raised in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, there was a videotape prepared to memorialise in some ways the service of your regiment in Bosnia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In exact detail, two ITN technicians created a video for a sergeant who saved their life as a thank you to him, and they took a series of film from ITN network and put tracks of music to it and gave it to that particular sergeant. His company commander then used the picture to -- used the video as a commemoration -- that is the wrong word, as a momento of the tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did that tape contain footage of actual events that occurred in Bosnia during the tour of one Cheshires?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I am very familiar with that tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have viewed it personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What I would like to do, your Honour, is play a tape which has previously been played, exhibit D58. It is in three segments and I would ask that it be played one segment at a time. We will pause after each segment, Colonel, and then I will ask you, among other things, whether you recognise any portion of that segment as having been taken from the Mostar tape which you have described. Very well, if we could play the first segment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could hold the tape for a moment, first what you have seen so far, Colonel, do you recognise it as having been taken from the Mostar tape that you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Parts of are, parts of it are not. The original tape is 90 minutes long and I know it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could call back the image that was on the screen when we paused, do you recognise this segment as being from the Mostar tape, produced by ITN for a soldier in the 1 Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to confess I do not remember that particular bit, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the vehicle type in this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, it is a -- I cannot actually tell if it is one of our own and the timeframe. It is certainly a British army Scimitar working for the United Nations. Whether it is one of our own or not, I cannot see the call sign markings on the side from this angle, so I could not identify that. If it was taken during the period November until May, it would be one of ours. If it was taken afterwards, it would be one of the PWO's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any other way of assisting us to identify the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is certainly an UN vehicle and as I said, if you could tell me when the tape was taken I could place it in context. I cannot put this piece of picture in context. It appears to be somebody either handing up a shotgun or handing down a shotgun.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You do recognise the weapon as a shotgun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is not an UN-issued weapon, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could continue with the tape, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is the second segment. Did you recognise portions of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I think we are talking about two different tapes here. This is not the tape that I was referring to earlier that was given to Sergeant Kudavinski, which was adopted by A Company as their tape. This appears to be an amalgam of footage from television, and it is not the tape I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you recognise Lieutenant Colonel Thomas in the second segment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could play the third segment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could freeze there, if that is possible, do you recognise that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Whose is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a Warrior. Do you mean whose actual vehicle is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know, can you tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the commander officer's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does it appear to be firing in this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually know the circumstances and I viewed that whole piece of film. I know it is returning fire at two HVO soldiers who have just fired a RPG-7. If you look at the earlier part of the picture you will see the RPG-7 impacting on the wall just to the right of the Warrior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Maybe we can turn back and see that, if that is possible. If we could go forward now, please? 22

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see it impacting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You can point it out on the brick wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we could go back to the brick wall, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you able to determine the impact of the round?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see the smoke of the round just there (indicates). When you look at the whole piece of film, you actually see the impact of the round, and the contact report that was sent was that they had been engaged by a RPG-7 and had returned fire at the firing position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know where and when this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it occurred during the monitoring of the cease-fire after 21st April. I could be wrong. I cannot remember the exact village, I just remember the piece of film, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Who has the complete tape of that event, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The complete event was shot by television, I do not know which company owns it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That will complete the viewing of the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I just make a point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You played that piece of film backwards. Could you play the piece of film backwards showing the soldiers in the Scimitar in what appears to be passing a weapon down to soldiers, because I think is a very misleading bite of film which makes it appear that United Nations soldiers were actually passing weapons down to the warring factions within Bosnia, and I find that to be quite a dreadful piece of film. What I am saying is if you play that film backwards the soldier is having it passed up to him, and if you were to look at a larger piece of film and put it in context, you would see exactly what is happening in that piece of film, and I think you will find the soldier passed the shotgun he was carrying up to the soldier in the Scimitar to have a look at and the soldier in the Scimitar passed the weapon back down to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have that tape? Do you know where we can find that tape, a larger tape of that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Who would have that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen that piece of tape, I think the Prosecution have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We have it, judge. This tape has been edited and we are more than willing to play it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that is a slight procedural problem, Colonel. Perhaps we can leave that for the response of the Prosecutor when he can ask the context of this video on which the witness was questioned, and then we can have it shown. However, Mr. Hayman, this proves that the witness has the impression that he is being asked to respond on the basis of very partial material, but the judges are here to appreciate what is being shown, and we are able to say things which we do not always want to. First of all, Colonel, I quite understand your remark. It will be up to the Prosecutor, who is in charge of his case, to refer to it in his re-examination, and then he can ask for the previous part of the tape to be played. Thank you. Continue, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have played everything we have pertaining to that incident, your Honour. If there is another more complete tape, we would certainly welcome it being presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, on that line, it begs the question as to where this tape came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I could continue with my examination, your Honour, I would like to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you can continue your cross-examination, but the question will arise as to the source of this video, which we have already seen. It seems to me that we have already seen these three sequences.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, this tape and the film was shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: By whom and during which testimony, please? Do not hurry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was when Tudor Ellis was testifying on 30th September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It has been admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, it has not been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So it is still under the previous reservation that we had for some documents. Mr. Hayman, if I remember well, I think Mr. Hayman said that he reserved the right to give the source of this video later, was that not so, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We did, we also showed the tape to Captain Ellis to see what portion or portions he could authenticate, and we are doing the same thing with this witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, you got the answer of the witness, he has not identified everything and for the moment we will not admit it into evidence until it has been identified, and we will retain in the record the reservations expressed. Perhaps if we had seen it in its totality, we would have a completely different understanding, precisely the question of who was handing the weapon to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, yesterday you discussed a criticism you had of Colonel Blaskic for not arresting any suspects whose names he may have relayed to the military prosecuting authorities within the HVO, or up his chain of command, if you will. I would like to ask you if you have undertaken any study of the law in the former Yugoslavia or in Bosnia that would set forth what the standards are for referring suspects for further investigation and possible prosecution, as well as the standards for arresting a soldier who may be the subject of that type of procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had not. I was only applying the regulations that exist in our own army and in the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But you would agree those are not regulations that would have applied on the territory of Central Bosnia in 1992, 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The law of England did not apply to soldiers in the former Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The law of England did not, no, but the Articles of War did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Tell us. Within United Kingdom military law, is the same standard of proof required for referring an individual to a military prosecutor for further investigation and for arresting and detaining an individual? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, what I am saying is that if I was commanding an organisation that had or was accused of committing an atrocity the like of Ahmici and I knew, I would initiate an investigation with all the resources at my command, and if I identified people who had been involved in it, yes, I would arrest them and I would detain them pending further investigation by our military police authorities. That I am entitled to do as a commander. I would certainly not want those soldiers continuing to operate under my command if I suspected them of doing such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is there a procedure under UK military law for further investigation directed by the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is, by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Under some circumstances under UK military law are those suspects detained, and then under other circumstances not detained, pending that investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you telling this court that the UK military law requires a suspect to be detained under certain circumstances and not under others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are certain circumstances in which a suspected person is required to be detained by our regulations and the remainder of that area of jurisdiction is up to the judgment of the commanding officer or the brigade commander, or the divisional commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You are talking about an area about which under UK military law there is discretion in the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We are not talking about a violation of UK military law, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would consider it a severe error of judgment by a commander, but technically, he has that jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let us return to 16th April for just a moment and then I will conclude. I am going to approach, your Honour, with permission. Directing your attention back to Exhibit 29J and the overhead transparency upon it, and calling your attention to 16th April, you drew two blue lines to indicate the separation lines, if you will, of the HVO and then two additional lines to indicate the withdrawal points, if you will, of the BiH following the cease-fire of 21 April 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, on 16th April 1993 how far towards the line marked "A" did the HVO advance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a recollection that line A was significant within the requirements of the HVO, and I think it marked the forward limit of quite a long-standing HVO presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Sorry, you believe the HVO advanced across the line marked "A" on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they had positions up there in the hills dug in and they advanced along the valley floor, was our reading of the battle as it was reported to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At what time was the maximum advanced or securing of territory north of the spinal road from Vitez to Busovaca achieved by the HVO? Was that on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the major attack started on the morning of the 16th and there was continuous fighting in that area through the 17th and 18th, but the major offensive appeared to be on the morning of the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When would the maximum amount of control of territory have been achieved by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would suspect by the end of the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In relation particularly to the village of Ahmici, how far north of the spinal road did the HVO go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were, I would say, about line alpha, as far as we could determine. We did not actually patrol into that area. As you can see, there are no roads and we did not take our Warriors. There are roads, but our Warriors had terrible problems getting up them. They are very small roads. It is quite mountainous.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the location of Barangaj, above Ahmici on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that place, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Kratine, is that a location you believe was overtaken by the HVO on 16th or 17th, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kratine is shown as a ridgeline. We understand the HVO were in positions up on these ridges by the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond or just up to the ridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a Croat village, to the best of my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Poculica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and there were certainly Croat positions up here and Jelinak was held by the Croatians as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are there other villages in the Lasva Valley within canton 10 that were not the subject of fighting or conflict on 16th, 17th, 18th, 19th April and so forth 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. We asked those questions yesterday, I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The question was asked yesterday, Mr. Hayman. Change your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How many villages are there, if you know, in the Lasva Valley area, within the canton 10 designated region of either Muslim or mixed Muslim Croat population? Ten or 100 or 200? Can you give us an estimate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are dozens of them, you can see them on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Many, many, many villages, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On 16th April, how many Muslim or mixed Muslim Croat villages were attacked by the HVO in the Lasva Valley? Were they all attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not all attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were ones adjacent to the spinal road from Vitez and Busovaca and Kruscica which we have already discussed, are those the villages that were attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These are the questions that were asked yesterday, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And there were others as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The same objection and the judge is telling you, change the question, Mr. Hayman. These questions have been asked in one way or another. You may have changed the form, but the judges are aware of what you are doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They were not asked, your Honour, and the record will speak for itself. One moment. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Not in that form, that is true, Mr. Hayman. The previous question was put in that form, but I agree with you that this one was not put in that form, but I am saying that the judges are fully aware that you are trying to put the same question in a different form, so let us not play around with words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is not my intent, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am convinced. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, other than the villages along the spinal road from Vitez to Busovaca, and other than Kruscica which we have discussed and Stari Vitez, what other villages not adjacent to the spinal road were attacked on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, this is the ground that we covered when counsel was going through the list of these particular villages yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I asked about three or four villages, your Honour. Now I am asking an open-ended question to end the inquiry and I think I should be allowed to do that, despite counsel's repeated objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Listen, I propose, Mr. Hayman, that you put for the last time an open-ended question on a subject that was discussed yesterday. We are prolonging the debate unnecessarily. The day will come when we will fix a period of time for each party. The parties do not have every right in proceedings. The Trial Chamber also has certain rights and it is its responsibility to guide the debate within a certain time period. Tell us exactly what is your objective and then the Trial Chamber will know whether that is in line with that objective or not. It is 12.52. We are going to end this cross-examination this morning, so please choose your questions and we are stopping at 1.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have stated the question, your Honour, although it continues to be interrupted so the witness cannot answer. I will state it again and if Mr. Kehoe will abstain from objecting, I can conclude my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is not Mr. Kehoe, it is the judge who is speaking to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, other than Kruscica and Stari Vitez which we have discussed, and other than the villages along the spinal road from Vitez to Busovaca, namely Ahmici, Santici, Pirici, Nadioci and others, what other villages did you observe, or did you hear reports of, within the Lasva Valley were attacked on the morning of 16th April 1993? Can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the morning of 16th April 1993, they were the villages that we initially had reports were being attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume work at 2.30. Mr. Prosecutor, you have your right to re-examine, after which the judges will have their own questions. The meeting is adjourned until 2.30 pm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume the hearing now. Please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I would like to remind you that your rebuttal must follow very strict limits and you are not to start the principal examination again, but simply limit yourself to make any clarifications or rectifications of points you feel should be clarified or supplemented in light of what took place during the cross-examination. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, could we turn to the documents to your right on the table which are the documents that Defence counsel introduced during his cross-examination. They relate to various excerpts from 1 Cheshire Mil Info Summs. Do you see those, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The first one is Defence Exhibit D59, that is 19th January 1993, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next to that document, and you can take it out of the sleeve, is what we would call a draft notice, a call-up order, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This was before you arrived in Bosnia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This particular Mil Info Summ that has been related by the Defence counsel, and I am reading seven lines down, the sentence beginning with, "the recruitment", do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you read that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The recruitment of civilians, i.e. people who have no involvement in the BiH/HVO forces, is a reflection of the assessed need by the BiH forces to strengthen themselves against the perceived increased threat from the HVO."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stop there, Colonel. Later on that month, was there in fact an attack by HVO forces against the Muslims in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So this particular assessment was correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was indeed a threat against the Muslims by the HVO at that time, and that initial period of our deployment in Vitez was dominated by the interethnic fighting in the Kiseljak valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn ourselves to the next exhibit that is to your left in the sleeve. Again, could you take that out of the sleeve?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you speak more slowly, please? The interpreter has not finished interpreting the witness's answer, and here you are quickly rushing into a second question. We want to save some time, but that does not necessarily mean that we have to speak as quickly as that. We are trying to work with the proceedings, not only about speaking faster. Go ahead, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President, your Honours, and I apologise to the booth. Let us turn our attention to D60. That particular document is dated on 18th April 1993, again a 1 Cheshire Mil Info Summ, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On this particular Warrior -- this Warrior call sign reflected a checkpoint at grid reference 134001, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to double check the map, but I think it is just south of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you check the map very briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a BiH checkpoint just to the east of Travnik which had been put in place after -- initially during the tense period following Boban's visit on 8th April and then reinforced and strengthened after the HVO attacks on the morning of the 16th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it had been there some time prior to 18th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Turn the page . Annexed thereto is the four paragraph cease-fire signed only by Blaskic; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned on cross-examination that you did not see any such document signed by the Bosnian forces, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you to your knowledge or anybody within the British battalion or the ECMM monitors, did anybody negotiate any such cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at this point on 18th April. We had been negotiating with brigade commanders continuously in the school, and this is the first time we had seen, to my memory, a document from Colonel Blaskic's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this point, the date 18th April 1993, would it have been to the strategic and operational advantage of the HVO to sue for peace on this date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we first saw it, we initially thought, "thank God, a bit of sanity is returning to this place" and then realised quite quickly that it really was not a valid document. The key thing that was missing was any suggestion that the HVO forces would withdraw to former lines of conflict. It appeared a rather crude and naive attempt to seize land in an operational offensive and then sue for peace when you had achieved your objectives, with no intent within your statement of your cease-fire document of relinquishing that land you had captured. So we did not give it any validity at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was there any reference in this document signed by Blaskic to give up any ground that he had gained and that the HVO had gained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is no mention at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise, let us go to the last document -- excuse me, not the last document, I believe it is Exhibit D65. If you could refer to the back of it, you can see the numbers on there, Colonel, the exhibit stickers on the back. So do you see that particular reference on D65, beginning with, "Colonel Blaskic claimed that there had been a BiH offensive on the area, contravening the cease-fire"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it your conclusion, Colonel, that he was complaining about a cease-fire when there was in fact never any agreed cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is complaining about the cease-fire document that he had sent to us, we had not seen any cease-fire document signed by the BiH, and it was usual, and it had been the case on 17th, 18th and 19th, for negotiations to proceed such a cease-fire involving all parties to agree it, so this appears to be a claim by Colonel Blaskic that his offered cease-fire or the document which he had signed stating there was a cease-fire had been contravened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the last of those documents, Colonel. I believe it is, for the record, D67. That is the one with the Mil Info Summ 180 for 28th April 1993. Do you have that before you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It refers, does it not, to a village, Kazagici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Kazagici was a Muslim village, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you visit Kazagici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I visited Kazagici on 28th April, 27th or 28th, some time around there. At that point, the cease-fire negotiated on the 21st was largely being honoured in the Vitez/Kiseljak, Busovaca area, but south of Busovaca in the Kiseljak valley, the cease-fire seemed to be being totally ignored by both sides and that had become our main area of effort in that time, to try and bring that cease-fire to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were asked on cross-examination whether or not the destruction in a village could be caused by collateral damage, and I think you responded that a village could be destroyed by collateral damage?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With all due respect, your Honour, that was not the question and answer that occurred during my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Would you perhaps modify your question, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. You went to see this village, correct, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On 28th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember reporting over the radio that a great many of the houses had recently been burnt, and by that, I mean they had been torched, systematically destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that similar to the houses that you saw torched in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Santici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in various other locations in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you conclude when you were there that the Muslims torched their own houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It is a daft question. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going back to some questions that were asked by Defence counsel during cross-examination concerning what Blaskic and whether Blaskic fulfilled his responsibilities in putting together a list of soldiers responsible for the massacre in Ahmici, do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did that list indicate to you that these were HVO soldiers who were on this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did, although initially Colonel Blaskic accused the Serbs of attacking Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So was there a change in his position from the Serb to this list of HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever find out directly or indirectly during this time that Blaskic claimed that Muslim HOS units from Zenica committed this crime in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about Muslim MOS units from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are saying Muslim people attacked Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is right. Did you ever hear Blaskic maintain that Muslim people attacked Muslims and burnt their houses and murdered them in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, but if I had I would have considered it as ridiculous as the accusation that the Serbs had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it was practically impossible for the Serbs to do it and why Muslim people should shoot and murder themselves is just -- it defies any logic that I can think of, and also there were statements made by some of the refugees --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Colonel. Your Honour, there is no testimony that the accused ever said this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment. Things are going so fast here. I have to understand the interpreters. I am still listening to the interpretation of the witness's answer. I would like things to go more slowly so the judges can understand and then listen to you with all respect that would be due to you. Has the witness completed his answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, what is your objection? Please do it calmly, slowly, so that it can be interpreted properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I apologise to the witness and the court for interrupting, but I think the question is impermissible. The question initially was: did Blaskic ever blame MOS, some Muslim group; witness: no. Question: would that have been a ridiculous accusation, and we were hearing a recitation as to how it would have been absurd to blame MOS for the attacks when the witness said Blaskic never blamed MOS for the attacks. It is not relevant, that is my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I sustain that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I be heard on that, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course you can be heard. Nonetheless, I do feel that the objection is well grounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. However, if I might say that based on the questions given by Defence counsel, this particular issue has become an issue, this particular question has become an issue and we will present evidence that in fact Blaskic did maintain that Muslims from Zenica murdered these people in Ahmici. My question at this point is with his varied responses, first the Serbs and then the HVO, I think it is probative at this point whether or not Blaskic blamed Muslims during this timeframe as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Bear with me a moment, Colonel, I am just going to shift from topics, because obviously we are not going to cover everything covered in cross-examination. I will shift topics at this juncture and move ahead to troops and the number of troops. You were asked some questions on cross-examination about whether or not the number of troops that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had outnumbered the number of troops that were in the employ, if you will, of the HVO. Do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I could not remember the exact numbers, but I was aware that the BiH outnumbered the HVO in terms of numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As a lieutenant colonel in the British army, in examining such issues over the course of your career, is the number of troops on each respective side an accurate assessment of how strong each individual army is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is too simplistic a measurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can look at the Korean war where small groups of British soldiers held out against mass wave attacks of Chinese and North Koreans. The numbers are not actually relevant, it is more to do with the other factors of combat power and these are the actual fire power, direct and indirect, available to the commander; the state of motivation and morale of his troops, which we call the moral aspect of fighting power. There are a great many measurements of military capability before you would be in a position to assess which is a greater force. Sheer numbers is just simplistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The fire power in the Lasva Valley and in Central Bosnia, who had the upper hand in fire power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croats without a doubt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please wait for the answer. I am not able to hear the answer being completed and there you are already asking the question again. The judges do, after all, have the right to hear the entire answer. Please think about the French-speaking judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I apologise. Going back to my question, Colonel, who had the upper hand in fire power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO had the upper hand in fire power and had greater access through their munitions factories within Vitez to ammunition and artillery and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see any weapons such as the size of a 40 millimetre anti-aircraft weapon being used by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I actually saw one in Busovaca, a 40 millimetre anti-aircraft cannon mounted on a flat bed truck, with an enormous amount of 40 millimetre ammunition. It is an extremely formidable force multiplier in terms of the devastation it can cause in a ground role. I certainly would not want to go up against it, even with my Warriors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to Dario Kordic. You discussed on direct and cross-examination the issue concerning a convoy being diverted to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who diverted that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldiers in black uniforms was how it was relayed to me, which I presumed were the people who lived down in the cottages, as they were called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were these the individuals --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I personally debriefed the officer who led that convoy because it was so badly conducted. He said that the soldiers who hijacked the convoy, when challenged by the fact that Colonel Blaskic had given permission for that convoy, moving from the depot in Zenica up to Travnik, a soldier said, "we do not take our orders from Blaskic, we take our orders from Dario Kordic".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did that incident relate to that particular convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the abducting of that convoy. It later transpired that Dario Kordic did not believe that the Croat community within Central Bosnia, and specifically Busovaca, were receiving a fair share of the available aid and so he instigated the abducting of that convoy into Busovaca to bring aid to the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Had you had any experience of Kordic doing that before that or after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. When convoys had been hijacked by HVO forces in the past we had rung up the headquarters of Colonel Blaskic and he had secured the release. I can think of a very specific convoy of flour and yeast that he returned to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that an isolated incident, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my experience, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to Dario Kordic, you attended various meetings where Blaskic and sometimes General Petkovic were present, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was Kordic at any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also participated in cease-fire negotiations, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And were there when documents were signed concerning cease-fire negotiations, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was Kordic there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he sign those agreements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to those individuals who diverted that convoy, other than this particular diverting of a convoy to Busovaca by Kordic, was there any indication to you that those soldiers were otherwise not under Blaskic's command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That incident led me to believe that they did obviously take orders from Dario Kordic, so they seemed therefore to respond to a parallel or different chain of command on that occasion. I have no reason to believe in our studying of the HVO forces within the Lasva Valley that they were not under the routine command of Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were present during the negotiations on 21st April 1993 with Petkovic and Blaskic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the negotiations, was an issue raised concerning whether Kordic would go along with any agreement that was reached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. I cannot remember the exact circumstances. I may even have raised it myself because of this confusion of Kordic being able to interject in this kidnapping of this aid convoy. I wanted to make sure that when we had a cease-fire agreement signed by Colonel Blaskic that Dario Kordic would honour the conditions of that cease-fire and was not some form of rogue missile in Busovaca. General Petkovic made it quite clear, in his inimitable way, that Dario Kordic would do as he was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am sorry about the pacing, Mr. President. I will slow down as much as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are excusing yourself with the President, but do it for the interpreters as well. It is very difficult to interpret if you work under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, you were asked on cross-examination with the easel about a chain of command that moved from the operative zone to the operative group down through a brigade level.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And down to what you would call ground troops, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Down to the lowest chain of command, a section in the British army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that a normal chain of command in the British army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the chain of command in the British army, division, brigade, battalion, company, platoon and section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What does a commanding officer in your capacity, Colonel, or in Blaskic's capacity, what do they delegate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They delegate the tasks, in the form of mission statements, and they delegate the resources to complete those tasks. What they do not delegate is the responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Explain that, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whoever is the commander who sets the overall mission is responsible for the planning and conduct of that operation, and he will be given the resources to conduct that operation for the number of brigades he has, or battalions or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, could you slow down a little bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. He will conduct what we describe as an "estimate", which is a decision-making progress, until he comes up with his plan. He will then construct a set of orders based on his plan. He will then give those orders to his subordinates to execute his plan. That does not matter whether it is a divisional plan, two or three star General level, the brigade commander's plan, the battalion commander's plan, the company commander's plan as we discussed before. It depends on the size of the objective and the resources. Implicit in the plan is the intent of the commander and the commander remains responsible at whatever level he has set the goal to ensure that the plan is conducted according to his orders, and his responsibilities are to check that is the case with his chain of command which functions throughout the battle. The commander does not go away when the battle starts, he stays and fights the battle and puts himself in a position where he can influence the effect of his plan as it unfolds on the battlefield. He remains responsible for the conduct of that plan and the success or failure of the operation, and the conduct of his troops conducting that operation. That remains his responsibility. In summary, you can delegate the task, but you do not delegate your responsibility. That is why you are a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Accordingly, would it be fair to say, Colonel, that Blaskic or you yourself have to take steps that your orders are carried out in the way that you want them carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You train your force to do that, and one of your responsibilities as a commander is to train and discipline your force to conduct the operations in the way you require them to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, does this include following mandates of the Geneva Convention and the Articles of War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does and that is reinforced in my own army with a mandatory requirement every year for all ranks, from the highest to the lowest, to actually be formally taught the Geneva Convention. You conduct all your operations according to the Geneva Convention, otherwise you are a war criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is the requirement, Colonel, of a commander who is giving an order to attack to protect civilians in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is implicit in the Geneva Convention, and it is one of the paragraphs in our orders card, so when a commander gives a set of orders, we have an aide memoire covering the paragraph headings that he must address within his orders according to our doctrine, and in "service support", which is the final generic paragraph heading, one of the listed factors he must take into account in both his plan and the execution of his plan is refugees. They are implicit in his plan, how he is going to deal with the refugees, how he is going to protect the refugees. It is an extremely difficult thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So after a battle has been completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, before a battle is completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Hypothetically before, is his responsibility to civilians, both before, during and after a battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are attacking, your plan must address and you must allocate the resources within your plan to address how you will ameliorate the effects of your attack on the civilian population that may or may not be in the area. Equally, after the attack, you have to allocate the resources to look after the civilians and you may well injure or kill some of those in your attack. That is one of the costs of war, but you must, and you are required by the Geneva Convention, to treat them and the enemy as your own when they are wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting, but I would like to note that this subject of protecting civilians and avoiding civilian casualties in wartime was not gone into on cross-examination by me. This is new material, and the problem with raising new material on redirect is if we, the Defence, do not have the opportunity to cross-examine, we are deprived our right, the accused's right to cross-examine on this subject matter at all, so I am raising it for the court, I think redirect should be limited to matters raised on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I take a quick look at my colleagues here, who tell me that I really have to answer, something which I would answer anyway. Yes, I think that is true. If you ask a question in a rather general way about the situation of the British army, the way it is trained, the way it carries out orders, the way it respects the rights of civilian populations and refugees, that is one thing, but if you go into too long a development of this point, that does deprive the Defence, who only very slightly touched on that subject. You deprive them of the right of reply. Since we do not have this right, I ask you now to move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were asked, Colonel, with regard to conversations that the British battalion had with Blaskic regarding the 400 civilians outside the garage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, and I remembered that we were requested or told, I am not sure which, by Colonel Blaskic to deal with the snipers ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Under the Articles of War, Colonel, contrary to you dealing with the snipers, whose responsibility was it for those civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic's forces attacked Vitez that morning and implicit in what we have just talked about was Colonel Blaskic having resources and a plan to protect and look after those refugees and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he appear to want to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, it is difficult to remember one's exact emotions four years ago, but I remember being quite horrified at the prospect that these HVO soldiers who were shooting at these Muslim civilians were now about to be attacked and possibly killed by the United Nations UNPROFOR. That is not what we were there to do and we were very reluctantly did it, especially against the backdrop of a great deal of accusations on the part of Colonel Blaskic's headquarters as to our attacking Croats, which was patently untrue, and supporting the BiH offensive, which was patently untrue, and now being told by him that if we wanted to protect the refugees, then we ourselves should attack his forces. We did it; very reluctantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Blaskic was put on notice about these civilians outside of the garage, and you were asked some questions by Defence counsel concerning the work of ICRC and the conducting of the investigation involving a massacre in Ahmici and other issues; do you recall those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Blaskic had prisoners in custody shortly after the battle, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
