utterances.text: Yes, we knew of at least two prisoner locations. One was in the cinema complex in Vitez and the other one was in the Dubravica village, I think in the school. There were a large number of prisoners held by both sides at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you believe, Colonel ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did I believe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am just waiting for the translation, if you will. Did you believe, Colonel, based on the information that you had, that Blaskic had the means at his disposal to conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic was the regional military commander. Within his organisation he had military police, he had within the witnesses -- sorry, within the prisoners he had people from that village, and it was blatantly obvious that he had the means and the ability to conduct an investigation, he just did not appear to have the will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again on cross-examination you mentioned ICRC.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And their requirement not to disclose information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. It is core to their entire work that they have to remain bluntly impartial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After 16th April, were members of the ICRC complaining to Blaskic and everyone else about prisoners being forced to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, their two greatest complaints to the United Nations was their ability to access areas of confrontation, and on various times we provided them with Warrior support to move round the field of battle, and the other vociferous complaint from ICRC at the time was their lack of access to prisoners held within the Lasva Valley, specifically in Dubravica school and in Vitez, which they believe was absolutely contrary to the Geneva Convention, as the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So with this information concerning digging trenches and access to prisoners, did Blaskic appear to do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Appear to do anything about access to prisoners, or digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he appear to want to stop the forced digging of trenches by prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think at that stage it had become a matter of virtual survival at the tactical battle, as the momentum of the Muslim advance came. I do not think the Croats had the resources to dig trenches and were utilising their prisoners to do that. I cannot comment on the state of Colonel Blaskic's mind over that issue, but on the ground, we saw no manifestation of an order to rescind the illegal use of prisoners for digging trenches. It was a major issue with the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During your time there, you described previously the truck bomb in Stari Vitez on 18th April as a terrorist act. Did you see any steps taken by Blaskic to investigate that terrorist act?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to the shelling of Zenica, following your phone call from the British battalion to the Hotel Vitez, did you see any steps by Blaskic to investigate the shelling and killing of civilians in Zenica on 19th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, other than there was another engagement of Zenica on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did his failure to protect the civilians at the echelon, stopping the digging of trenches, the truck bomb and the shelling of Zenica, was his failure to do that consistent throughout this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not appear to address those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he demonstrate any desire to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I was aware, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were the second in command at that time, were you not, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I also know the commanding officer was entreating Colonel Blaskic to actually do something about it, and was very disappointed at the lack of response to this entreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again I am going to change subjects, Colonel. I want to raise with you the tape recording that was played by the Defence just prior to lunch. You recall that, do you not, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you detect a certain insinuation emanating from that tape regarding the conduct of the British battalion and specifically 1 Cheshire in Bosnia during your tour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That piece of film was similar to pieces of film that had been broadcast on Croat television during the period 17th to about 28th or 30th April, alleging that the United Nations and specifically BritBat were actively supporting the Muslim offensive against the Croat peoples, and pieces of edited film from the world's media were being put together to illustrate these accusations, and we had seen a great deal of these pieces of film in their entirety and were outraged, actually, that this crude black propaganda was being exercised to discredit us, and the only logical conclusion we could draw is that if the Croat government were able to discredit us, then the accusations that we at the time seemed to be the only people making of these massacres would lose validity, and it just appeared a very simple piece of propaganda, more akin to the sort of thing that was perpetuated in the former Soviet Union than in a democratic country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did Blaskic engage in that propaganda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He sent many faxes and made accusations on the phone, some of them personally to me, as to the conduct of our soldiers, such allegations as wantonly and indiscriminately firing our 30 millimetre cannon in the centre of Vitez, which was an absolute lie; faxes alleging desecration of the catholic church in Vitez, which as many of my battalion, including myself, were Roman Catholics, as well as myself, we found absolutely appalling, and general assistance to the BiH by the movement of weapons and soldiers around the battlefield in support of the BiH offensive. The whole thing was absolutely ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, did you think the insinuation from the tape was that British battalion and British soldiers were arming the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is exactly what it looked like it was trying to show to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did it ever happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no it did not. We were quite ruthless in ensuring that our people did not gain a particular allegiance of sentiment with any particular one of the warring factions. To do that, we moved our companies, with the exception of B Company in Gornji Vakuf, around Bosnia so that our soldiers would realise that within this extremely savage and complex civil war there really were no good guys and nobody that actually deserved their personal support. There were only victims and aggressors and who the victims or the aggressors were really depended on the ethnic balance of the area they were working in and no single warring faction had a monopoly on being the victim or the aggressor. That was a message we were determined our soldiers would understand. The idea that we would arm either faction, Serb, Croat or Muslim, was ridiculous. It just is an insult to the work that we were doing there, the things we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There was also a clip -- excuse me. There was also a clip played by the Defence of now Lieutenant Colonel Martyn Thomas standing in front of a burning building. Could you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the soldiers of 1 Cheshire burn villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We are about to review a tape which for the record, Mr. President, your Honours, is numbered Prosecutor's Exhibit 112. Does this tape --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. I would like to confer with my colleagues. (Pause). Mr. Kehoe, excuse us, because we wanted to confer about the questions we will ask in a little while. For the time being, please continue. I think you wanted to move to the video now, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could just have the witness state who is speaking on the video; if you could, Colonel, who is the one speaking on the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is Mr. Martin Bell, a BBC defence correspondent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this particular video clip is a BBC video clip. This particular clip was given to Defence counsel and we have a transcript in both French and English, and at this point before we do play the videotape, I would just ask the court if I could hand out this particular transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is a translation in French?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Do you have a copy for the interpreters, please, in English? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, if I could go to this videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could ask the video booth to go back to the segment where the shotgun is being examined by the British soldier, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you stop there, please? If we could go to the beginning of that, please? The beginning of the first frame where the weapon is up in the top of the vehicle, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stop right there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, was that portion of the tape on the tape shown to you this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The portion of the tape where he was looking at the weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was the part where he was handing it down to the Muslim soldier, handing it back to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What does the commentary reflect that the British soldier was doing with that weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had obviously asked the BiH soldier if he could have a look at it, not an uncommon thing at all. It was a soldier who was curious to look at a weapon that was unusual to see. The AK derivative weapon systems were in common use throughout Bosnia, it was quite unusual to see a pump action shotgun, which is not really an infantry weapon. I would have done the same myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is likewise reflected in the transcript, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bell says that the soldier is inspecting, having a look at the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is a little different, Colonel, from handing out weapons to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is just my point. That is just straightforward propaganda in that previous piece of film.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you consider that first time you were shown this morning misleading?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President? (Pause).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact I would probably even use stronger language, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, again this particular tape we just showed was offered to the Defence, acknowledged by Mr. Nobilo in April 1997, and we have no further questions of this witness. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Before giving the floor to my colleagues and after having conferred with them, I would like to turn to Mr. Hayman and call to his attention and Mr. Nobilo as well, that is to both the Defence counsel, indirectly to Mr. Blaskic as well, to Rule 85 of the rules. In 85, I would like you to look at paragraph C which says that the accused may, if he so desires, appear as a witness in his own Defence. I turn to you, Mr. Nobilo and Mr. Hayman, you must decide, in light of several things that were stated by Colonel Watters throughout his testimony, you are the ones who have to answer this question, but would you like Colonel Blaskic to appear as a witness before us, that is under oath, in his own Defence, given the fact that we will not go back to Colonel Watters. If you would like to confer about this, of course do, speak together and speak with the accused as well, of course, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that General Blaskic speak now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am suggesting that if you like, you can have, in his own Defence, Colonel Blaskic appear as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is a question I am asking. You should answer. I am asking you whether you would like that Rule 85(C) be used, stating that the accused may if he so desires appear as a witness in his own Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We expect he will, but we will not make that decision finally until the Prosecution's case is concluded and whether we see if after we bring motions to the court whether the motions are dismissed, after the end of the Prosecution's case, or whether the Defence must even put on a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I know that in your system that is how things are done. In my own, things are done very differently. In fact, after each testimony, the accused is invited to speak about what was said, because things are clear, they have just been said, and that, of course, once -- I am not asking you, I am simply calling your attention to this provision of the text. The fact that the trial is this long, when you want to, in a year or a year and a half, maybe quite a while from now, together with my colleagues and without making any suggestions, I simply wanted to draw your attention to Rule 85(C). I have understood your answer that for the time being in any case you do not wish to make use of Rule 85(C) and to ask in a separate application that you will, if you later on decide that you want to, call your witness. Do we agree with that then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for advising us of your interpretation of Rule 85(C). It had never occurred to me, coming from my system, that the accused might have the opportunity to rebut each Prosecution witness who states they had personal dealings with him, or perhaps even other witnesses. It is something that Mr. Nobilo and I have never discussed, nor have we discussed it with the client, but we will do so in light of your comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I will now ask my colleagues whether they have any questions they wish to ask Colonel Watters. First, Judge Riad. Have you any questions that you would like to ask? The floor is yours. Excuse me, I would like us to settle the tendering of this video clip. I suppose it will be tendered as evidence, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I apologise for not doing that earlier, but I would offer that into evidence as a Prosecution exhibit, number 112.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 112 and the English would be 112A and 112B. If you would allow, I would also like a decision to be made about the transparent film which is on the easel, that is the Defence Exhibit D61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We offer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge Riad. It is your turn to speak now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Watters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judging by your long military experience and your first-hand knowledge of the events which took place in this critical period, you may be in a condition to clarify some, I would call global issues, without perhaps going into small technicalities. My first question is: was the HVO a regular army, a disciplined army, or was it a gathering of undisciplined factions? As simple as that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personal observations and in discussions with members of the HVO, and paying due cognisance to the majority of the commanders having served in the regular JNA, it had all the organisation and trappings of a disciplined regular military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My second question is: was General Blaskic the undisputed commander of this, what you call it, canton 10, the regional commander, or was he in no condition to command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He represented the HVO forces at all negotiations I attended and in my presence related directly to his superior officer, General Petkovic, so I am quite clear that Colonel Blaskic was the military commander, HVO, Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You related various major actions which I am not going to repeat, but it goes from artillery shelling of civilians with what you called an unprecedented scale; let us say destruction of civilian houses in what you qualified as ethnic cleansing; civilians digging trenches; officers ordering people out of their houses under threat of killing them, and other major actions. Could such major actions be taken without the knowledge of the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in my opinion, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could it be taken without his consent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Isolated incidents could happen without his consent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were some of these isolated incidents or was it some kind of organised enterprise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The co-ordination of the activities specifically on 16th and 17th April, in my experience, could not have happened without a great deal of planning and co-ordination at the relevant level, sir. There was too much going on at the same time for it to be spontaneous or out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It seems that not all the Muslim villages have been attacked, some of them were spared. What was the criterion of the choice of what you call the ethnic cleansing? Why did they choose, for instance, Ahmici and not other places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a conundrum, sir, that I do not think I have ever got to the bottom of. The logics that I believe were applied were the ethnic cleansing of the Muslim villages on the boundary of the proposed Vance-Owen Plan canton 10, which ran between the Travnik/Vitez/Kaonik road and Zenica, embracing Travnik, which itself was strange, being a Muslim village. The second was the securing of that route within Central Bosnia, linking the major Croat centres of population, and the other reason for the devastation in Ahmici was the idea that Ahmici was very special to the Bosnian Muslim people, as I explained in my evidence, and looking at the other terrorist operations such as the lorry bomb, a brutal and savage lesson to the people of Ahmici would aid the ethnic cleansing in the remainder of the Lasva Valley by terrorising the people to leave, and it certainly worked. They were terrified and they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned Ahmici. I recall now that you said that it was a holy place and it was perhaps a gathering of holy people. What was the purpose of destroying the holy people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To terrorise the remainder of the Muslim people living in the environs and show them what would happen to them if they did not leave, and if it had happened to Ahmici, then it could happen to all the other Muslim villages. If you terrorise one village, sir, then the amount of military effort and terror you might have to apply to subsequent villages will be less, because they will be in absolute terror of their lives, as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did it have any cultural and religious value in the area, Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We understood that it did, as a town that produced a higher proportion of holy people, of mullahs, to the Bosnian Muslim religious community. It had a special place in the minds of people as a holy town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the towns which have been destroyed, there were Croatian areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why were not the other Croatian areas destroyed? Was it so minutely and deliberately, let us say, attacked and the shelling was very clearly addressed to certain parts, or was it just indiscriminate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw evidence of shelling in Ahmici, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The other places.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the artillery shell and the mortar are not a very accurate weapon, and it is very difficult to judge where they will fall. It would have been impossible, really, to use artillery and mortars in mixed villages without inflicting collateral damage in areas you did not intend to attack. It is not a precision weapon, it is an area weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you mentioned that the houses of the Croats were safe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was specifically, sir, in Ahmici. It was a very stark difference between the Croat end of the town and the Muslim end of the town. The Muslim end of the town had just ceased to exist and the Croat end of the town was as if nothing had happened, it was surreal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Speaking of the truck, the bomb truck explosion, what was the dimension of this truck explosion? Was it on a military, let us say, size or could it be a private endeavour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on a tarmac road. The crater was very large. The devastation to the houses was very large. It was certainly no smaller than, I would say, 1,000 pounds of explosive, given my own experience. I would not really know, sir, the access there might be to quantities of explosives like that in Vitez. Our view was that it was part of a continued intimidation of the Muslim people, and was a further -- it was out of character, sir, of what we had seen up to then of Croat forces and it was shocking from that point of view. We do not know who did it, it reinforced the operation that was ongoing with the HVO and it continued to contribute to their actual tactical effort. I would not -- I have no personal knowledge of who actually drove that bomb into the middle of an occupied Muslim area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Shahbuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHBUDDEEN
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to take you back to this episode concerning the shotgun. What was the nature of the vehicle which appeared in the photograph with this shotgun? Was that a Warrior vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, that was a reconnaissance vehicle, which in the British army is known as a Scimitar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Scimitar. Now then my question to you is this: would a shotgun be the type of weapon which was likely to be taken around in a Scimitar vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, there is no room inside a Scimitar for anything but the commander and gunner and their personal weapons, sir. A very small, tight vehicle. The idea of transporting weapons in a vehicle like that is just not practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is the range of such a pump action shotgun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be lethal at about 30 yards, sir. Beyond that, it would degrade to about 100 metres, where it would be largely ineffective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that kind of weapon of substantial use in a military confrontation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are certain applications in close quarter fighting where a shotgun would have a degree of military utility, sir, but in terms of a weapon that is carried in my own army, no, it is not carried by the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How does the use of such a weapon compare with the use of a military rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is just no comparison, sir. I would not want to take on a man with a military rifle with a shotgun. I would lose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You spoke of Kruscica, and my recollection tells me that you said that in your memory you saw nothing leaving Kruscica but that you saw, and I noted down your words, "an enormous amount of RPG mortar and artillery coming into Kruscica". Would I be right in supposing that you were referring there not to the weaponry itself but to the shells launched by weapons of this kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You remember a portion of your testimony, I think you were talking about the ICRC and the inhibition which that organisation has against divulging information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My recollection is that you said something to the effect that the HVO were given no information from victims and survivors of Ahmici from which they could further any investigations; is my recollection correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I think I said, sir, was that the HVO were given no information from the ICRC as to statements they had received from the survivors of Ahmici. The major problem for the ICRC was accessing the survivors, the majority of whom were prisoners of the HVO at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I see. So would I be right in understanding you to mean that whereas the HVO got no such information from the ICRC, you were not saying that the HVO had no information at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I certainly would not say that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You remember that counsel asked you about certain HVO soldiers who stood outside of the Hotel Vitez and were pointing their rifles, I think, in the direction of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were asked whether that implied that there was a military threat from Stari Vitez. You remember that phase?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is this: what was, in your assessment, the substantial purpose of the military action which the HVO took in relation to Stari Vitez? Was the purpose to respond to a military threat in Stari Vitez, or was the purpose to remove the civilian population of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it was probably both, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Both, good. Let me ask you a question about Ahmici, Santici and Nadioci. You visited those villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see any evidence of defensive positions in those villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see any evidence of the population in those villages being capable of presenting a military threat to anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me take you back --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just clarify that, are we talking about when I visited it after --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was the only time that you visited. What I mean is if there had been previously any defensive positions installed in those villages, would you have expected to see traces of those defensive positions at the time when you later visited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would, sir, and I did not. I did see defensive positions in other areas, but not in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me take you to your interesting presentation on the various levels of command, strategic, operational, tactical; I think those were the three which you referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be possible in some circumstances for a senior military officer to operate partly at one level and partly at another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in operational terms it would probably be quite confusing, sir, if he was to do that, because his subordinate commanders would de facto be removed of their command if he commanded the subordinate units as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: From the point of view of your military experience, and your knowledge of military doctrine, it would not be usual for a commander at the strategic level also to operate at the operational level, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, sir. He would give direction to his operational commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us talk a little about the organisational arrangements of the HVO within Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you in the course of your stay become aware of the existence of a HVO communications system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let me put this to you. Given your knowledge of the area and of the existence of that communications system, was General Blaskic likely to be aware of what was happening in Ahmici, in the other places, regardless of whether or not he was in Vitez or in some other place within Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know if he was, sir, but he would have the means to communicate with his subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He would have had the means to enable him to be kept in touch with any developments, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Whether that would be on radios, and the distance from Vitez to Ahmici is quite small and the HVO carried small communications systems with them, I would say it would be very fair to assess that in certainly the immediate environs of Vitez, Colonel Blaskic would have been in radio contact with his forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you in a position to assist the court by giving an estimate as to within what period of time General Blaskic would have been in a position to learn of what is happening in Ahmici on 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be confident in saying that Colonel Blaskic would have monitored his operation, and monitored the success of that operation, and in his formal military training, and I am sure he would have applied that, as I would do, I would have placed remits on my subordinates to inform me at certain schedules as to what they have achieved against the timeframe I had set them for their various objectives. I would expect Colonel Blaskic to have that situation in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would that explanation apply also to Nadioci, Santici and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would I be right in summing up your testimony to mean this, that on 16th and 17th April 1993, you either saw or were reliably informed of a number of acts of violence occurring in different places at approximately the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would I be right in understanding you to be also saying that there was a common pattern running through those incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that that pattern included the use of military force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we observed and I personally observed infantry assaults.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it likely that a military unit on the Croatian side could have been involved in those operations and acting wholly independently of General Blaskic's command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not the impression I gained at the cease-fire negotiations, sir. I do not think it is practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You remember you spoke of some press men, who I think came to you in the early hours of 16th April. They were newspaper men, TV men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were journalists, newspaper people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they local journalists or foreign journalists, or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I see. I take you back to this piece of testimony concerning, shall I say the list of suspects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Which General Blaskic said, I think to Colonel Stewart, that he had had prepared and submitted upwards through his chain of command; you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also spoke of Ahmici being followed by, I think I have your words, "media and world attention", mm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So there was Ahmici, there was some publicity. I would not put words in your mouth; could you relate the presentation of that list of suspects to this media and world attention? Did the media and world attention occur before the list of suspects was presented, at the same time when the list of suspects was presented, or after the list of suspects was presented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say during, sir, because the media interest lasted for actually quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I see. It was not a one-off affair.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I see. You spoke of Colonel Blaskic saying to the authorities of BritBat that they could shoot at the snipers who were assaulting the refugees outside of the BritBat echelon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the snipers were shooting and killing the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: First of all, did Colonel Blaskic say, if he said it, that he did not know how those 400 refugees came to leave their homes. Did he say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that, your Honour, no. It was really the urgency of the situation, that these people were being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would I be interpreting you correctly this way: BritBat was a neutral military force interfacing with two military forces which were in confrontation one with another; would that be a way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, yes, sir. We were also, in the north, between the Muslim 2nd Corps and the Serbs, but in the Lasva Valley that is exactly the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your force was part of or associated with the United Nations exercise, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we were part of the United Nations forces in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In a normal conflict involving the use of armed force, like a major war, is there any military force which interfaces with both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of it, sir. It was certainly an unique experience for us in the European theatre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHBUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel, I have two or three clarifications I would like to ask, since there were a number of questions already asked by my colleagues. I would like to go back to the issue of this document, 60, having to do with the cease-fire, this well known cease-fire, about which you said that in your opinion and in the opinion of the other members of your staff was not valid. How would you characterise, in light of this period when you were in command of that Central Bosnia mission, how would you characterise what criteria, if you like, would be used for a cease-fire to be valid, because you have rejected it by saying not only was it not applied or implemented but it was not valid in your opinion, there was no validity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The lack of validity, sir, is attributed to the fact that this was the first time we had ever received a cease-fire declaration down the single chain of command of the warring factions. This document was not known to the BiH and its production had not followed the usual, and by this stage quite often repeated procedure, of the level that issues the joint declaration have sat with ourselves, UNHCR, ECMM, and have actually produced a consensus and out of the consensus comes the terms of the cease-fire. These terms were promulgated only by the HVO and only under the signature of Colonel Blaskic and did not have the co-signature of Enver Hadzihasanovic, who was the commander of 3rd Corps. That had been the usual procedure, we had done it at the brigade level and at the regional level before this. So that is why I do not think it was valid, and it certainly was not viewed as valid by the BiH and it did not manifest any change at all on the ground, other than a series of communications from Colonel Blaskic's headquarters alleging contraventions by the BiH of this cease-fire, which they were not committed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you consider that it was a kind of a propaganda document to be used for the international community or world opinion, or do you believe that it was a document to be used for strategic uses, an unilateral cease-fire, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My personal view was that this was part of a strategic plan that the HVO, having conducted their pre-emptive attack on the morning of the 16th, hoped by issuing this cease-fire document on the 18th that the gains they had achieved would be frozen and that they would succeed in their endeavour and that the United Nations would assist and enforce this cease-fire. That was quite a naive strategic plan, but it did certainly serve the purpose afterwards as being a document which Colonel Blaskic's headquarters were able to quote ad nauseam as to concentral inventions of this cease-fire, but the key, the A to D in this document, were the normal measures placed into a cease-fire document. The one that is missing, which is the fundamental one, is that the opposing forces would withdraw to their previous lines of fighting, which was the implicit and practical measure that achieved success on 21st April when I illustrated on the map the blue lines, sir, to separate the opposing forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Colonel, at the negotiating tables, you often met with Colonel Blaskic. Did you ever speak about the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recollect discussing those, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Last question: the HVO soldiers, would you agree with me, say, that they had been more or less trained either in the former JNA or with the Croatian military forces; would you agree with that opinion? This is a question I am asking you, it is a question I would like to ask you first before I get to the other question. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could apologise and go back to the previous question, which I did not fully grasp. Did I discuss with Colonel Blaskic the Articles of War; not in terms of an intellectual debate, but in terms of the implementation of cease-fire agreements we certainly did, especially in terms of the meeting on the 21st, and exchange of prisoners and access to prisoners by the ICRC was a fundamental condition under that cease-fire. Your second question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me ask for that clarification. Would you agree with me when I say that the HVO soldiers had been trained militarily either in the former JNA or more recently with the regular Croatian forces? Would you agree with that first statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority of the commanders I met, I know them to have been former JNA officers. I cannot give a personal account of the individual soldiers, sir, I did not talk to them about it, but they were certainly trained by their military commanders. We saw them training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is my question: at the headquarters, from what you know now, had military manuals, both in Croatia, and specifically of the former JNA, dealt with applications of the Geneva Conventions at all levels of command, as well as respect for the laws and customs of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly the JNA, and Yugoslavia was a signatory to that Convention, sir. I did not read JNA tactical pamphlets. I do not read Serbo-Croat, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel, the Tribunal would like to thank you for this long and patient testimony which you have been willing to provide. You can now go back to your command, to your units. I believe that it is now time to take our break until 4.30. I believe that the following witness is a protected one, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So not to lose time, perhaps during the break and five minutes before the judges come in, the witness could be brought in once the curtains have been drawn. Perhaps the usher before the judges leave could accompany the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is suspended. We will resume at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, please bring in the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, your Honours. My next witness is Witness F, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We are going to ask the Registry first to verify the identity of the Witness F, who is going to remain seated and who is going to read her solemn declaration, but please I want to make sure of the identity of the witness so that the Prosecutor and the Defence are aware of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness F, you have been called by the Prosecution in the trial against Colonel Blaskic, who is here present. You have come and we are fully aware that it must be very difficult for you to come here. You know that you are addressing a Tribunal and that this Tribunal is going to listen to you with the greatest of attention. You are first going to answer questions put to you by the Prosecutor, who has called you, after that I wish to remind you you will be answering questions put to you by the counsel for the Defence, because all the accused in all judicial systems are entitled to Defence counsel. Of course you are protected by very strict protective measures that have been undertaken, and that is the reason why you will be known anonymously as being Witness F. If in the course of your testimony, there are names that you do not wish to pronounce, or elements of identification which might even indirectly enable your identification, we are here ourselves, the Prosecutor, the Registry and we have technical means to remedy anything that may occur and that may be considered an error. Therefore please speak without fear, as serenely, as quietly as you can. Mr. Prosecutor, Witness F is ready to answer your questions now. No, please remain seated, but first the Registry is reminding me that you have to read the declaration, but this time, remain seated in doing so. WITNESS F (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President and counsel, what I propose to do is ask a few preliminary questions and then moved for a closed session, because some of my questions may result in the identification of Witness F. If I may begin, Mr. President, with some background questions: Witness F, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you born in Vitez and raised in the village of Pirici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a high school graduate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if at this point I could move for a closed session, I will try to expeditiously move through a series of questions and then we can return to an open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We are at the court's disposal, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. My colleagues and myself feel that we should go into closed session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness F, when you arrived at Niko Vidovic's house, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, the lady in white uniform was standing there and there were two stands there, one had the IV and the other one had blood. I passed by and went to the basement and Croatian women and children were there, they were all my next-door neighbours. I entered and there were beds placed there, there were five of them and then there was also a stove and there was some food being cooked there. We were told to get in and Ivica told us to stay there. He talked to us, he was saying that the best solution for us would be for us to stay there in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, Witness F, that preparations had been made in advance for accommodating a large number of people in the basement of that particular house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Croatian women and children were all dressed up, it was cold that early in April, they all had coats and some hats. My children were in their pyjamas and I was barefoot, I only had slippers on my feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Finka Vidovic you have identified as wearing a white sort of outfit. Do you know what she did, was she a nurse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she was a medical nurse. I do not know what she was doing on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did it look like medical supplies had been positioned at Niko Vidovic's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after about an hour, Finka arrived with a bundle of medicine which she put on a table in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue with your observations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was terrible shooting going on outside from all kinds of weapons, I am not an expert in weapons, but I know for instance that there was large calibre weapons being shot as well as small. I was very agitated and my children as well, we were all in fear, we were standing next to a small window, it was open ajar for some fresh air, and I could feel the smoke that was coming in. I knew that something was burning. The men were not there, there were only women and children there. However, occasionally they would come in, the men did. They would come to check on their families and Ivica told us that we must not leave the basement, even if we needed to go to the bathroom. Around 9.00 or 9.30, I am not sure about the time, I had to take the little one outside and I asked a woman if I could take her outside. She told me to ask Ivica. The first time he said that I could not and the second time I asked another man and he said that I could, so I passed by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did you go? Did you stay in the house or did you go outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went upstairs and got out. As I was coming out, I saw soldiers in black and camouflage uniforms. They were eating something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you notice any kind of patches or insignia on those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I passed by them and they were not paying any attention to me. They probably thought that I had taken shelter there just like the rest of the women.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What badges did you notice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It said "Vitezovi" and the others said "Jokers".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many soldiers did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were more of those in black uniforms, maybe four or five in black uniforms and three or four in camouflage uniforms. They had some unusual hats, they were round with a red fringe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you hear any conversations among those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were talking about some accomplished task, they were happy, they said that everything was done. At the moment when I came out, because there is a staircase, you had to climb the staircase to get out, I saw Ahmic Sulejman, Eso and Cazim's houses on fire. I took the little one to the toilet and on the way back, I saw Frano Vidovic, Anto Kupreskic and Anto Dudzo, they were talking. Anto Kupreskic was an older man, he was in uniform though and he had a rifle and some grenades, and the other two did not have any weapons and Frano had a white insignia on his sleeve. He was pointing to the basement where we were, and he said, "we should not kill them, because some of us may get killed. We should protect them". Then I thought we were imprisoned here. Then I came down and I told my brother, "we are imprisoned here", and he nodded to me because he was standing next to the window and overheard them talking. I also came over to my husband and told him everything as well and then we knew what actually was going on. A few moments later, a boy of 12 or 13 came running, I knew him all my life --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a second before you recount that particular incident. You said you had seen Hazim's, Eso's and Sulejman's houses burning. Were those houses in the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were near the stadium, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They appeared to be on fire when you saw them on the morning of 16th April, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue with your testimony. You were relating an incident with a young boy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he ran into the basement, opened the door and the fire, the shooting was still going on outside, it had died down a little bit from what it was at 5.30. Then he addressed to the Croatian women and he said, "you know what is new?", they said, "what is new, Jure?", that was his nickname. "All the Muslims were killed. I personally was at the stadium and I turned over two Muslims, Muharem and Nedzad", they were two cousins. At that moment, I had an attack of something, I started screaming, I wanted to get out, go out and find Nedzad and Muharem. Finka did not allow me to go out. She said I should sit down and not make any problems and gave me a tablet to take to calm down. Then my husband who was watching this took the older daughter and told me to go out, he said that if they were going to kill us, then we should come out and be killed as people are not as mice. I took my little one and started out. However, Ivica who was standing outside in front of the door told him, "go back and stay there where I told you to stay, because you do not know what is going on". Finka also asked my husband, she pleaded with him, "go back, it will all change, it will not stay like this". My husband was excited, then we stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were there in the basement and you remain in the basement on the 16th, did you hear the husbands of any of these women come in and mention their successes? Can you tell the court exactly what you heard them say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the husbands were not in the basement, they would come down occasionally, Satko Vidovic came in, that is Anto Vidovic, called Satko, came in at one point and said a friend of his, Fahrudin Ahmic, was killed and he was sorry he was killed. However, when they would come in, they would not address us, they would talk to their wives. They were talking how they were advancing and at one point, Ivica, called Jevdjo, entered and said, "women, victory is ours. You should not be afraid. It is almost over". The women were applauding, they were rejoicing and they were saying they had no losses themselves. Then they started talking among themselves, I remember a young man came to see a young woman from Busovaca and I overheard them speaking. They said that the job was done, and Ivica said that this match had to be played at some point, and, "we are victorious". He was talking to this young woman and he said, "this is ethnic cleansing and I think we will succeed pretty soon". Ivica said, "we do not need to go to Zenica at all, we can just stay in our Herceg-Bosna". We were just listening to what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned some individuals, you mentioned Anto Vidovic, known as Satko. How was he dressed on the morning of 16th April, as you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he have any insignia on him that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned an individual by the name of Ivica "Jevdjo" Vidovic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wore camouflage pants, a blue jacket and throughout the time he carried a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see any insignia and/or markings on him that identified his unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there any reference by Jevdjo as to who his particular commander was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). Then he told him, "just sit where you are, because if it were according to Nenad, you would not be sitting where you are sitting".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, did you also hear any conversations about a rocket launcher being fired on Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please tell the court what you heard in respect of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica came down to the basement, his nickname is Jevdjo, and he told the woman, "women, our own are advancing so do not worry about anything. Seven rocket launchers are shelling Kruscica and soon Kruscica will be ours".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he say seven rocket launchers or a seven barrelled rocket launcher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, VBR, which means barrelled rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did anything else happen that particular day in the basement that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted), I do not know where he had been, but his brother Drago came and was talking to his mother who had been sitting there all the time. She started crying. She started crying and shouting, "Ivica, my son, my flower", we did not know what she was referring to. Then the people started whispering, "Ivica was killed", then Drago looked around at us and he said "if somebody needs to cut throats, I am the one who is going to do it". That is how we understood it, Ivica Vidovic, her son, was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How was that individual dressed who discussed cutting throats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had the old JNA coat and a white band on his sleeve and he carried a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he have any insignia on him that you could remember at this date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you stay at that particular house the night of 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we stayed there the 16th , in the night of the 16th, we stayed there all night. The morning of the 17th came, some Croat women were going out and then were coming back. The shooting was dying down, in fact it had stopped altogether. At one point we asked Ivica when we were going to come out and he said that we still had to wait, that there was no question about our going out. It must have been very light, it must have been around 9.00 already. Ivica came in and said to the women who were present there, who were sitting around, he said, "women, go and look for your men and tell them that I cannot protect them alone by myself any more like I used to, because the Jokers and the Vitezovi found out that we are protecting some Muslims, so it is my head in question now". Then a young woman got up and said, "do not put your life at risk", and then he said, "when we talked about it, you were all for protecting them, but now the Vitezovi and the Jokers found out, nobody wants to do anything".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Witness F, was that on 18th April, because I am asking you questions about the 17th April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this was on 17th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you also, did you see an individual by the name of Stjepan Vidovic on 17th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he come into the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He entered the basement, he spent the night of the 16th in the basement, but on the 17th he went to see his house, and he came back. His wife stayed there all the time and he was talking to her and other women who were there. He was saying that the minaret of the mosque had collapsed, that various houses were burned down and that his own house was left intact. He said that he saw a tractor going to collect Muslim bodies on the roads and around the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did he say about the condition of all the Muslim houses that he had seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He seemed to be rejoicing, because his own was intact and all the Muslim ones were burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he say anything about Muslims coming back into the area again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said nothing but nobody could go back, because everything was still burning, but he said that they were going and he meant Croats, that they were going in a tractor and collecting the bodies, the Muslim bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now you mention that Ivica "Jevdjo" Vidovic had come in and he said the Jokers and the Vitezovi had found out you were in this particular house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said he turned to the women, but he was speaking aloud so we could all hear him. He said, "Jokers and Vitezovi have found out about you here", so he said, "women, go and find your men, because I cannot do anything on my own. When we were all making a decision, we were all for it, that we protect them, and now nobody wants to do anything. Now it is my head that is at risk", and he showed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica left and some women were talking. One said that she did not know where her husband was, another one did not know where her husband was and they told us to go to another room, because there were two rooms in this basement, there were some blankets there, but we needed the blankets so we remained standing all this time, but he left. In the meantime, another neighbour of ours came. He approached my brother -- this was about two hours after Ivica had left. He was looking at my brothers, my husband, myself, all of us, because we were all together. He offered them cigarettes. I approached to see what was going on, what he was going to tell them, and he said, "I am really sorry, but I was ordered to bring you out. I was ordered by them". He stood there, they all smoked a cigarette, all of them, he still was standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say he was ordered by them, what did he say he was ordered to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They ordered him to bring out the three of them. He said, "I have to bring the three of you out so that you would be killed".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say the three of them, I take it, is that your husband and your two brothers who also would be in the particular house with their families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened after he informed people -- informed your brothers and your husband that they had to be taken out to be killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he told them, he lit a cigarette with them and then stood there for a while, and at that time there was a sound of a personnel carrier approaching. I heard the personnel carrier arriving in Niko Vidovic's yard and somebody in the English language is calling out my brother's name and the surviving Muslims and Ivica Vidovic said there were no surviving Muslims and there were no civilians in the basement and that they should feel free to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did that UNPROFOR vehicle leave then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were there for about 15 minutes and then they returned. I heard that. They were our last hope, when this UNPROFOR left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness F, you indicated that a man by the name of Anto Pudja had come to the basement to talk to your brothers and had informed them he had to take them out in order to have them killed. How was Anto Pudja dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wore a black hat and a camouflage uniform, and he was not looking -- he did not look happy. He looked sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he have any particular insignia on him identifying his unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. What happened after he left the basement and after this UNPROFOR vehicle that had come to that particular location left? What did you and your family members and your brothers and their families do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was going on throughout the day of the 17th, they were coming and talking, and would go out, they were bragging about their victories. The night came, the night of the 17th, and a woman came running in, and shouted that the barns were on fire of Plavcic, and that they should go towards Rovna because they may be in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was Plavcic a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was in Mahala, as we called that section. That woman was outside and she must have either seen it or been told by someone. Then the basement started emptying, people started leaving one by one. Then in the end we were left alone, just my brothers there and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So after information was passed to the Croat people in the basement that a Croat barn was burning, the Croat women and children in the basement left and you and your families were left alone, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said that the Croat people in the basement fled in the direction of Rovna, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were saying that that was the most secure place to go, so they hurried there, and we were talking what to do, we could not turn and go towards Pirici, we could not do that, so we decided to go to Rovna, and so we started. As we were coming out, there were two soldiers in front of the house, they were also in a hurry, they were picking up knapsacks from the ground, they were all leaving in a group so we joined this group too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you fled along with the Croats in the direction of Rovna, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that on the morning of -- was that on 18th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you go in the direction of Rovna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We went ahead and we followed. They went ahead and we followed. There were bullets flying past us, we were going towards Pirici, then we kept going and going. We crossed the river, then some of them split off and some to another, so we were left alone on the road, my brother was ahead and I had my daughter --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness F, I am going to interrupt you for a minute, please, because you are going a little bit fast. When you left the house of Niko Vidovic and you went toward Rovna, did you go down the road past Nenad Santic's house, which is indicated as number 5 on Prosecutor's Exhibit 113A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you cross the Lasva river across a bridge and find a refuge in a house in the area of Rovna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you remain in that house the night of 18th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. That woman's name was Safradin and the Safradins are a Croat family, but when we went in, there was a neighbour of ours inside who recognised us and he was surprised how come we got there. Then he got lost, he went away somewhere. The woman was afraid that we were going to spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Witness F, when you say "we", are you referring to yourself, your husband, your two children, your two brothers, their families and their children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were six adults and seven children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So that particular night of the 18th you stayed in a house near Rovna, all of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, do we intend to go past 5.30? If we do, I can continue my examination; if not, I can conclude it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, not at all. The witness must be tired of having to tell us about all her suffering, so we will adjourn as usual. Before the Trial Chamber rises, perhaps the Registry could ensure a closed session so that the witness can be shown out, or would you prefer us to do that after the judges leave? So Witness F, please stay seated for the moment. I should like to remind you that we have no hearing tomorrow throughout the day, so we will be resuming our work the day after tomorrow, that is on 13th November at the usual time, that is at 10.00 am. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: on Thursday, 13th November 1997)
